objections.answer: He mediated a new covenant, as Moses the old, and will reign over Israel gathered. The likeness Moses names is the prophet speaking God's words, and Jesus said, "he wrote of me."

entries.subject: scripture
entries.title: John 14:16, "he shall give you another Comforter", read as a prophet to come or as a third person
entries.summary: Jesus names the Comforter in the next verse: "Even the Spirit of truth; whom the world cannot receive, because it seeth him not, neither knoweth him: but ye know him; for he dwelleth with you, and shall be in you." It was given to the disciples themselves, within days, at Pentecost, and dwelt in them; a man born six centuries later was seen by the world and abode with none of them. Nor is it a third person: it is the power of the Father, by which Christ himself would come to them, "I will come to you."

points.claim: The Comforter is the spirit of truth, unseen by the world, dwelling in the disciples.
It was given to those disciples within days, at Pentecost.
It would bring to their remembrance what Jesus had said, and guide them into all truth: it inspired the apostles' witness.
By the spirit Christ himself came to them: "I will not leave you comfortless: I will come to you."

objections.objection: The Greek once read periklytos, "praised one", which is Ahmad, Muhammad's name.
objections.answer: No manuscript reads so: every copy, thousands of them, reads parakletos, comforter or advocate, and John uses it of Christ himself.

objections.objection: The Comforter is called "he", so it is a person.
objections.answer: The pronoun follows the Greek noun, as wisdom is called "she"; the spirit is the Father's power, poured out and shared, as no person is.

entries.subject: scripture
entries.title: Moses, the prophets and the apostles wrote what they claim
entries.summary: Critics divide the law of Moses among later writers and date Daniel to the Maccabees, after the events it foretells. Jesus spoke of "the book of Moses" and said "he wrote of me", and of "Daniel the prophet": to set their writings late is to set his word aside. Daniel foretold not only the Greeks but Rome after them, and the Messiah cut off before the city and sanctuary were destroyed, which no writer of the Maccabees' day could see. The theory of the law's sources rests on style and names, which one writer can vary; it has never produced the documents it supposes.

points.claim: Jesus held Moses the author of the law, and Daniel a prophet.
The law says Moses wrote it, and the later books receive it as his.
Daniel foretold Rome after Greece, and the Messiah cut off before the city fell: events after any Maccabean date.
Scripture claims to be given by God through holy men, moved by the spirit.

objections.objection: Deuteronomy records Moses' death, so he did not write it all.
objections.answer: The closing words were added, likely by Joshua, as the book itself says Joshua wrote in the book of the law; a note at the end does not make the rest late.

objections.objection: Daniel's prophecy of the Greek kings is too exact to be prophecy.
objections.answer: That assumes prophecy cannot happen, which is the question. And the fourth kingdom, iron, and the Messiah's coming before the temple's fall, lie past any date the critics allow.

entries.subject: god
entries.title: There is one God, the Father, and Jesus is his Son
entries.summary: "Hear, O Israel: Yahweh our God is one Yahweh," said Moses, and Jesus said it again. Paul: "to us there is but one God, the Father," and "one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus." Jesus was born of Mary by God's power, was tempted, did not know the day of his return, died, and was raised by God; none of this can be said of God. He is the Son of God, not God the Son.

points.claim: God is one, the Father.
Jesus is a man, the mediator between God and men, and calls the Father his God.
He began at his birth: the holy spirit, the power of the Highest, overshadowed Mary, and therefore he is called the Son of God.
He was tempted, but God cannot be tempted; he died, but God only has immortality; he did not know the day, but God knows all.
He is subject to the Father, who raised him and exalted him, and will be subject to him when all is done.

objections.objection: Jesus forgave sins, which only God can do.
objections.answer: God gave him that power, and the crowd glorified God "which had given such power unto men." He passed it to the apostles in turn.

objections.objection: Jesus was worshipped.
objections.answer: The word (proskuneō) is bowing in homage, given to kings and to men: the servant fell down and worshipped his lord, and the false Jews will worship at the feet of the ecclesia. God commanded it of his Son, and it is to the glory of God the Father.

entries.subject: god
entries.title: Jesus shared our nature, and overcame in it
entries.summary: Jesus was made of a woman, partaker of flesh and blood, made like his brethren in all things, and tempted in all points as we are. God sent him in the likeness of sinful flesh, and in that flesh condemned sin by a life without sin and a death that ended it. He learned obedience by the things he suffered and prayed to be saved from death. His victory is ours because he won it in our nature, not in a nature beyond temptation.

points.claim: He was born of a woman, of the seed of David, partaker of flesh and blood like his brethren.
He was tempted in all points as we are, yet without sin; God cannot be tempted.
God condemned sin in his flesh: by his death he destroyed the false accuser.
He learned obedience, was made perfect, and was saved out of death by God.

entries.subject: god
entries.title: The holy spirit is the power of God, not a third person
entries.summary: The angel told Mary that the holy spirit would come upon her, "and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee": the two lines say one thing. Jesus was anointed "with the holy spirit and with power." God's spirit is everywhere he is, by it he made and sustains all things, and he gives it in measure: it is poured out, taken from one man and put upon others. Paul writes of "the spirit itself." It is God's own power, not another beside him.

points.claim: The holy spirit is the power of the Highest, by which Jesus was begotten and anointed.
By his spirit God is everywhere, and made and sustains all things.
The spirit is poured out, given in measure, and taken from one man to put upon others: things said of a power, not a person.
It is the spirit by which the prophets spoke, and by which Micah was full of power.

objections.objection: Jesus calls the Comforter "he" (John 14-16).
objections.answer: Comforter (paraklētos) is a masculine word in Greek, and its pronouns follow it. Where the noun is spirit (pneuma), which is neuter, the pronouns are "it": "the spirit itself beareth witness." Wisdom is "she" in Proverbs without being a woman.

objections.objection: Ananias lied to the holy spirit (Acts 5:3-4).
objections.answer: To lie to the spirit at work in the apostles was to lie to God, whose power it was, as to reject the apostles was to reject God.

entries.subject: god
entries.title: John 1:1, "the word was God", read as Jesus existing before his birth
entries.summary: The word is God's word, his spoken purpose, by which he made the heavens. It was with God as a man's word is with him, and was God's own, as a man's word is himself speaking. It became flesh in Jesus at his birth. Tyndale and the English Bibles before the King James wrote "all things were made by it." John's first letter uses the same phrase of a thing: "that eternal life, which was with the Father."

points.claim: God made all things by his word.
"With God" is said of a thing: the eternal life was with the Father, and was manifested.
The English Bibles before 1611 call the word "it".

sources.quote: All things were made by it, and without it was made nothing that was made.

points.claim: The word became flesh when Jesus was born.

entries.subject: god
entries.title: John 8:58, "before Abraham was, I am", read as the divine name
entries.summary: "I am" (ego eimi) is ordinary Greek: the man born blind says the same words in the next chapter. The Greek Old Testament's name in Exodus 3:14 is "he who is" (ho on), not "I am". Jesus had said Abraham saw his day and was glad: Abraham saw it in the promise. Christ was before Abraham in God's purpose, foreordained before the foundation of the world and manifest in these last times.

points.claim: The same words are used by the man born blind, "I am he."
Abraham saw Christ's day by faith, in the promise, as the faithful saw the promises afar off.
Christ was foreordained before the foundation of the world, and the glory he prayed for was given in God's purpose before it began.

entries.subject: god
entries.title: John 10:30, "I and my Father are one", read as Jesus being God
entries.summary: "One" here is the neuter hen, one thing, not one person: Jesus prays in the same words that his disciples "may be one, even as we are one." The verse before says his Father "is greater than all." When the Jews accused him of making himself God, he did not claim it: he answered from Psalm 82, where judges are called gods, and said he had called himself "the Son of God."

points.claim: He prays that his disciples be one as he and the Father are one: one in mind and purpose.
In the same breath the Father is greater than all, and gave him the sheep.
Accused of making himself God, he answered that Scripture calls men gods to whom God's word came, and that he had said "I am the Son of God."

entries.subject: god
entries.title: John 20:28, "my Lord and my God", read as Jesus being God
entries.summary: A week before, Jesus had sent word to the disciples that he was ascending "to my Father, and your Father; and to my God, and your God." Thomas, seeing him risen, saw God at work in him: "he that hath seen me hath seen the Father." The Old Testament calls God's representatives by his name: Moses was made a god to Pharaoh, and the angel of the exodus had Yahweh's name in him. John closes the chapter by saying why he wrote: that we might believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God.

points.claim: The risen Jesus called the Father his God.
The Father was seen in him: God was manifest in the Son.
God's representatives bear his name and title.
John wrote that we might believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God.

entries.subject: god
entries.title: Philippians 2:5-11, "being in the form of God", read as God becoming a man
entries.summary: Paul is setting an example for the Philippians: "Let this mind be in you." Adam, made in God's image, grasped at being as God; Jesus, who showed his Father's character perfectly, did not count equality with God a thing to be seized (harpagmos), but humbled himself to the death of the cross. "Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him": exaltation is a reward God gives, and every knee bows "to the glory of God the Father." A disciple cannot copy God laying aside deity; he can copy a man refusing to grasp.

points.claim: The passage is an example for the believers to follow.
Adam reached for equality with God; Christ did not, but humbled himself.
He showed the Father's character: he that saw him saw the Father.
God exalted him for his obedience, to the Father's glory.

entries.subject: god
entries.title: Colossians 1:15-18, "by him were all things created", read as Jesus creating the world
entries.summary: Jesus is "the firstborn of every creature": part of creation, the first of it, not its maker. The creation in him is the new creation: the passage goes on to call him the head of the body, the ecclesia, the beginning, "the firstborn from the dead." The things created are thrones, dominions, principalities and powers, the ordered rule of his kingdom, not stars and seas. "In him" (en autō) all things were created: God made all things new in Christ.

points.claim: He is the image of God and the firstborn of creation, the first raised from the dead.
In Christ is a new creation.
Thrones, dominions, principalities and powers are ranks of rule, given to him and his body.
God created all things; Jesus is the one he worked through.

entries.subject: god
entries.title: Isaiah 9:6, "the mighty God, the everlasting Father", read as the child being God
entries.summary: The child is born and the son given: God is neither. Hebrew names declare what God does, and often carry his name: Jerusalem itself will be called "Yahweh our righteousness," as the branch of David is. "Mighty God" (el gibbor) gives the title el, mighty one, which Ezekiel uses of Nebuchadnezzar. "Everlasting Father" is father of the age to come, who sees his seed and says "behold I and the children which God hath given me." The verse after says what brings it about: "the zeal of Yahweh of hosts will perform this."

points.claim: The child is born, and given: he is God's gift on David's throne.
God's name is given to his king and his city alike.
El, mighty one, is used of a man.
He is father of a seed God gives him.

entries.subject: god
entries.title: Matthew 28:19, "in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the holy spirit", read as the Trinity
entries.summary: To be baptised into a name is to be joined to what it stands for, as Israel were baptised unto Moses. The verse names the Father who sent, the Son who was sent, and the power by which God worked in him; it does not say they are one God. The apostles carried it out by baptising "in the name of Jesus Christ," in whom the Father's name is.

points.claim: Baptism into a name means belonging to it, as unto Moses.
The apostles baptised in the name of Jesus Christ.
The Father's name is in his Son.

entries.subject: god
entries.title: John 14:9, "he that hath seen me hath seen the Father", read as Jesus being the Father or God
entries.summary: Jesus is the image of the invisible God, "the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person": in his words and works the disciples saw the Father, who dwelt in him. He says so in the next verse: "the Father that dwelleth in me, he doeth the works." In the same discourse he says "my Father is greater than I", and soon after prays to him as "the only true God". He who prays to the Father, goes to him, and calls him "my God" is not the Father.

points.claim: The Father was seen in the Son because he dwelt in him and did the works.
The Son is the image of God, in whose face God's glory is seen.
In the same discourse the Father is greater, sends the Son, and hears his prayer.
The Father is the only true God, and the risen Jesus calls him "my God".

objections.objection: Father, Son and spirit are three titles of one person, Jesus.
objections.answer: The Father spoke from heaven to the Son on earth, the Son prays to him and was forsaken by him, and two witnesses are two: "I am one that bear witness of myself, and the Father that sent me beareth witness of me."

entries.subject: god
entries.title: Jesus is the Son, set above the angels, not Michael the archangel
entries.summary: Hebrews argues at length that Jesus is not an angel: "unto which of the angels said he at any time, Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee?" He was made a little lower than the angels, a man of flesh and blood, and was then exalted far above them, so that "all the angels of God" worship him. Michael is "one of the chief princes" and did not dare rebuke the false accuser; at Christ's coming the archangel's voice goes with him, as the trumpet does, without being him.

points.claim: No angel was ever called the Son, and the angels are bidden to worship him.
He was made lower than the angels, taking not their nature but Abraham's seed.
Raised, he was set far above every principality, angels made subject to him.
Michael is one of the chief princes, who did not dare bring a railing accusation; Christ is the judge.

objections.objection: He descends "with the voice of the archangel", so he is the archangel.
objections.answer: He descends "with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God": the trumpet is not Christ, and nor is the archangel whose voice accompanies him.

objections.objection: Michael leads the angels in Revelation, as Christ does.
objections.answer: Revelation's Michael is a figure in a sign; Christ in it is the Lamb, worshipped by every creature, which is said of no angel, and an angel refuses John's worship.

entries.subject: god
entries.title: Psalm 82:6, "I have said, Ye are gods", read as men becoming gods
entries.summary: The psalm rebukes Israel's judges, called elohim, mighty ones, as the law calls them, and goes on: "But ye shall die like men." Jesus cited it of those "unto whom the word of God came", to show it was no blasphemy for him to be called the Son of God. God was never a man, "I am Yahweh, I change not", and beside him there is none. The faithful will be raised immortal and share the divine nature, equal to the angels, but they remain the sons who worship the one God, not gods who rise to his place.

points.claim: Elohim is used of judges: the law sends a case "unto the judges", the same word.
These "gods" die like men: they are mortal judges.
Jesus used it of those to whom the word came, to answer the charge of blasphemy, not to make men gods.
God was never a man, does not change, and has no god before or after him.
The faithful will be made like Christ and share the divine nature at the resurrection, and worship God for ever.

objections.objection: "Partakers of the divine nature" means believers are deified.
objections.answer: They share his nature as children share their father's: holiness now, and immortality when raised. Children do not become the Father; "there is one God, the Father, of whom are all things."

objections.objection: As man is, God once was; as God is, man may become.
objections.answer: Scripture says the opposite: "from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God", and "God is not a man". Before him there was no God formed, neither shall there be after him.

entries.subject: worship
entries.title: Yahweh is worshipped without images
entries.summary: "Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness ... Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them." Israel saw no form when Yahweh spoke from the fire, so that they would make none. The prophets mocked the craftsman who burns half a tree and bows down to the rest; the idols have mouths but speak not. Paul told the Athenians that the Godhead is not like gold or stone graven by art, and John wrote, "Little children, keep yourselves from idols." Bowing to an image, whether called a god, a saint or an icon, is what the commandment forbids.

points.claim: The commandment forbids both making images and bowing to them.
Israel saw no form, so that they would make none.
Idols are the work of men's hands, and those who make them are like them.
God is not like gold or stone; he is worshipped in spirit and in truth.
Yahweh gives his glory to no other, nor his praise to graven images; there is no God beside him.

objections.objection: The image is only a help; the honour passes to the one it shows.
objections.answer: Israel said the same of the golden calf: "To morrow is a feast to Yahweh." The commandment forbids bowing to a likeness even when it is meant for God.

objections.objection: God commanded the cherubim and the serpent of brass.
objections.answer: He commanded them made, not bowed to; when Israel burned incense to the serpent, Hezekiah broke it in pieces, and did right in doing so.

objections.objection: The one God has many forms, and the images are of those forms.
objections.answer: Yahweh says he has no equal and no likeness: "To whom then will ye liken God?" The gods of the nations are idols, and the Creator is not one of the things he made.

entries.subject: worship
entries.title: Prayer goes to God through Christ alone, not through Mary or the saints
entries.summary: There is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, and he ever liveth to make intercession for those who come to God by him. Believers are bidden to come boldly to the throne of grace themselves. The faithful dead, Mary among them, sleep until the resurrection and know not anything; they cannot hear prayers. Jesus taught his disciples to pray "Our Father" and to ask in his name; the apostles prayed for one another while alive, but never to the dead.

points.claim: Christ is the one mediator and intercessor.
Believers come to God boldly themselves, in Jesus' name.
The faithful dead sleep, and know nothing until the resurrection.
Calling on the dead was forbidden in Israel.

objections.objection: We ask the saints to pray for us, as we ask a friend.
objections.answer: A friend is alive and hears; the dead do not. Scripture has believers pray for one another, never ask the dead to: "Abraham be ignorant of us."

objections.objection: The prayers of the saints are offered in heaven (Revelation 5:8; 8:3-4).
objections.answer: The saints in Scripture are living believers, and these are their prayers, rising as incense, as in the temple. The vision shows no one praying to them.

entries.subject: worship
entries.title: Mary was blessed, but needed a Saviour like all
entries.summary: Mary was highly favoured: the holy spirit came upon her, and the Son of the Highest was born of her. She called God her Saviour, offered the sacrifice for her purification, and was among the disciples praying after the ascension. Joseph knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son, and Jesus' brothers and sisters are named. When a woman blessed his mother, Jesus answered, "Yea rather, blessed are they that hear the word of God, and keep it." Scripture says nothing of her being sinless, ever virgin, taken bodily to heaven or a queen of heaven; with the other faithful, she awaits the resurrection.

points.claim: She was favoured and blessed, chosen to bear the Son of God.
She called God her Saviour, and offered for her purification as the law required.
She had other children after Jesus.
Jesus put hearing the word above being his mother.
The queen of heaven was an idol Israel was condemned for worshipping.

objections.objection: His brothers were cousins, or Joseph's sons by an earlier wife.
objections.answer: Luke has another word for kin, used of Elisabeth, Mary's cousin. Matthew names the brothers beside his mother, says Joseph knew her not till her son was born, and the Psalm foretells that Messiah would be "an alien unto my mother's children".

entries.subject: worship
entries.title: The bread and the wine are a memorial of Christ's death, until he come
entries.summary: On the night he was betrayed Jesus took bread and the cup and said, "this do in remembrance of me." Paul gives its meaning: "as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come." The first believers, baptised into his death, met on the first day of the week to break bread. It is a memorial and a fellowship, not a sacrifice repeated: Christ was offered once, and "by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified."

points.claim: Jesus gave the bread and the cup to be done in remembrance of him.
It shows the Lord's death until he comes, and looks to his kingdom.
The baptised met to break bread on the first day of the week.
Christ was offered once for all: there is no sacrifice to repeat.
It is to be eaten worthily, examining oneself.

objections.objection: Jesus said, "This is my body."
objections.answer: He said it holding bread, with his body before them; he speaks so of himself as the door and the vine. After the words the cup is still "this fruit of the vine," and Paul still calls it bread.

objections.objection: The mass is the one sacrifice of Calvary made present, not repeated.
objections.answer: Hebrews sets Christ's once against the priests' daily offering: "where remission of these is, there is no more offering for sin." The supper looks back to a finished work, and on to his coming.

entries.subject: worship
entries.title: John 6:53, "except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man", read as the bread becoming his body
entries.summary: Jesus explains his own words in the same discourse: "he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst," and "the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life." To eat his flesh is to believe and take in his words, the bread from heaven as the manna was. He spoke it a year before the supper was given, to a crowd who did not break bread, and the law forbade drinking blood, a command the apostles kept for Gentile believers.

points.claim: Coming to him and believing on him is eating and drinking.
Jesus says his words are spirit and life, and the flesh profits nothing.
It was spoken before the supper was instituted, to those who did not keep it.
The law forbade drinking blood, and the apostles kept the command.

objections.objection: The hearers took him literally, and he did not correct them.
objections.answer: He did: "It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing." Those who went back went back because they would not believe, as he said.

entries.subject: worship
entries.title: Christ is the one high priest, and his people are a priesthood
entries.summary: Under the law many priests served because death ended each one; Christ "because he continueth ever, hath an unchangeable priesthood," one that passes to no successor. There is one mediator between God and men, and every believer is of "an holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices." The ecclesia has elders and servants who care for it as examples, not a priesthood that stands between God and his people: "call no man your father upon the earth," and an overseer is to be the husband of one wife.

points.claim: Christ's priesthood is unchangeable: it does not pass to another.
There is one mediator, and he offered once.
All believers are a priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices.
Elders serve as examples, not lords over God's heritage, and none is to be called father.
An overseer was a married man; forbidding to marry is a mark of the falling away.

objections.objection: The apostles passed on their authority by laying on of hands.
objections.answer: They appointed elders and passed on spirit gifts, but no priesthood: Christ "hath an unchangeable priesthood," and the apostles' own office was to witness his resurrection.

objections.objection: The Aaronic and Melchizedek priesthoods were restored to men in these days.
objections.answer: The Aaronic was changed with the law, and Melchizedek's order is Christ's alone, held "after the power of an endless life."

entries.subject: worship
entries.title: The spirit gifts were given to found the ecclesia, and ceased with the apostles
entries.summary: The gifts of the spirit were given by the laying on of the apostles' hands: Simon saw "that through laying on of the apostles' hands the holy spirit was given." They confirmed the word while it was new, and with the apostles gone there were none to pass them on. Tongues were languages men understood, a sign to unbelievers. Today God's word is the spirit's sword, able to make wise unto salvation. The gifts will be given again in the age to come, the powers of which the first believers tasted.

points.claim: The gifts were given by the laying on of the apostles' hands.
They were given to confirm the word as it was first preached.
Tongues were real languages, heard by men of many nations, and a sign to unbelievers.

Paul foretold that tongues and prophecies would cease; many take "that which is perfect" for the completed word, a reading that is debated, but the gifts' passing with the apostles does not rest on it.
The word, now complete, is the spirit's work in believers.

objections.objection: Believers speak in tongues and heal today.
objections.answer: What is heard today is not a language of the nations, and the healings are not of the man lame from birth or the dead raised. Signs alone prove nothing: false prophets show great signs.

objections.objection: Joel's promise was for all flesh.
objections.answer: Peter said Pentecost was "that which was spoken by the prophet Joel"; its full outpouring belongs to the age to come, whose powers the first believers tasted.

entries.subject: worship
entries.title: Mark 16:17-18, "these signs shall follow them that believe", read as signs for believers today
entries.summary: Mark says how they were fulfilled: the apostles "went forth, and preached every where, the Lord working with them, and confirming the word with signs following." The same list has serpents and deadly poison, which no one now takes as a test, and which Paul survived on Malta. Even then the gifts healed at God's will, not at a believer's: Paul left Trophimus sick and told Timothy to take wine for his stomach. Signs prove nothing alone; false prophets would show great signs.

points.claim: The signs confirmed the word as the apostles first preached it.
The same promise includes serpents and poison, fulfilled in Paul.
Healing was not at a believer's will: Paul left Trophimus sick.
Signs alone prove nothing.

objections.objection: "Them that believe" means every believer in every age.
objections.answer: Then every believer would drink poison unharmed. The promise was kept in those who first believed, and Mark records it kept.

entries.subject: worship
entries.title: God does not promise health and wealth now
entries.summary: Paul warned of men "supposing that gain is godliness," and wrote that "the love of money is the root of all evil." Jesus taught his disciples to lay up treasure in heaven, and the apostles taught that "we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God." The faithful of old were sawn asunder and went about destitute, and Paul's thorn was not taken away. God has chosen the poor of this world, rich in faith, heirs of the kingdom: the reward is at Christ's coming, not now.

points.claim: Gain is not godliness; the love of money is the root of all evil.
Treasure is laid up in heaven, to be given at his coming.
The faithful suffered and were poor, and received not the promise in this life.
Paul's thorn was not removed: God's strength is made perfect in weakness.

objections.objection: John prayed that Gaius might prosper and be in health.
objections.answer: It is a letter's greeting, a wish for a friend, not a promise; John rejoiced most that Gaius walked in the truth.

objections.objection: "By his stripes we are healed."
objections.answer: Peter gives its meaning: he "bare our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness." The body's healing comes at the resurrection.

entries.subject: death
entries.title: Man is mortal; the soul is not immortal
entries.summary: Man was formed of dust and became a living soul, the same words used of the animals. "The soul that sinneth, it shall die." In death a man's thoughts perish; the dead know not anything. God only has immortality; man must seek it, and receives it at the resurrection, when this mortal puts on immortality.

points.claim: Man became a living soul, as the animals are living souls; he returns to dust.
The soul dies.
The dead have no thought or knowledge.
Only God has immortality; it is sought, and given at the resurrection.

objections.objection: Rachel's soul departed as she died (Genesis 35:18).
objections.answer: Her life went from her: the soul is the life, which is in the blood. Balaam and Samson both said, in the Hebrew, "let my soul die."

entries.subject: death
entries.title: The dead sleep until the resurrection
entries.summary: Jesus called death sleep, and woke Lazarus from it; Martha knew her brother would rise "at the last day." Paul comforted the Thessalonians not with the dead in heaven but with their rising when Christ returns, and said that without the resurrection those fallen asleep have perished. David has not ascended into the heavens; the faithful of old have not yet received the promise.

points.claim: Death is a sleep, and the resurrection an awaking.
The comfort is the resurrection at Christ's return; without it the dead have perished.
The faithful have not gone to heaven: they receive their reward together at that day.

objections.objection: Moses and Elijah appeared with Jesus at the transfiguration.
objections.answer: Jesus called it a vision, and it was a sight of the kingdom to come: Peter says they saw his coming in power and majesty.

objections.objection: Elijah went up into heaven.
objections.answer: Into the sky, by a whirlwind: no man has ascended into heaven, Jesus said. Years after, a writing came from Elijah to Jehoram, king of Judah.

entries.subject: death
entries.title: The grave and the valley of Hinnom are not a place of torment
entries.summary: Sheol and Hades are the grave: Jacob expected to go there, Job prayed to be hidden there, and Christ was there for three days. Gehenna is the valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, where carcases were burned; Jesus' words about it quote Isaiah on dead bodies. The wages of sin is death, not life in torment: the wicked become ashes, and death and the grave are themselves destroyed.

points.claim: The righteous go to the grave: Jacob, Job, and Christ himself.
The valley of Hinnom is a place by Jerusalem; Jesus' words of it quote Isaiah's carcases of the slain.
The end of the wicked is death and destruction.
Death and the grave are destroyed in the end.

objections.objection: Sodom suffers the vengeance of eternal fire (Jude 7).
objections.answer: Sodom is not burning now: it was turned to ashes. The fire is eternal in its effect.

entries.subject: death
entries.title: Man lives once, then the resurrection and judgement; there is no rebirth
entries.summary: It is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgement. Man comes from the dust and returns to it, and he that goeth down to the grave shall come up no more, until God raises him. The Bible has no round of births: a man is judged for the things done in his body, in this one life, and the hope is not escape from the body but its resurrection, made immortal. Jesus denied that the man born blind suffered for sin before his birth.

points.claim: Men die once, and after that comes judgement.
The dead do not return to this life, but wait for the resurrection.
Jesus denied that blindness from birth was punishment for earlier sin.
The hope is the body raised and made immortal, not freedom from bodies.
Sin's wages are death, and its remedy is forgiveness, not a debt worked off over many lives.

objections.objection: Jesus said John the Baptist was Elijah.
objections.answer: He came in the spirit and power of Elijah, as the angel said, and John himself denied that he was Elijah.

objections.objection: Rebirth explains why some suffer from birth.
objections.answer: Jesus refused that explanation. Suffering comes from a world under sin and from time and chance, not as punishment for a life no one remembers.

entries.subject: death
entries.title: Luke 23:43, "today shalt thou be with me in paradise", read as going to heaven at death
entries.summary: The thief asked to be remembered when Jesus came in his kingdom: he looked for the future kingdom, not heaven that day. Jesus did not go to paradise that day: he lay three days in the grave, and after rising said he had not yet ascended to his Father. Paradise is the garden, restored when the tree of life is given in the kingdom. Greek manuscripts have no punctuation, so "I say unto thee today" is possible; but Jesus' other sayings with "Verily I say unto thee" do not add "today", so grammar cannot settle it, and the case rests on the thief's request and on where Jesus was that day.

points.claim: The thief asked about Christ's coming kingdom.
Jesus was in the grave that day, and had not ascended after he rose.
Paradise is the garden of God, restored in the kingdom.

entries.subject: death
entries.title: Luke 16:19-31, the rich man and Lazarus, read as the state of the dead
entries.summary: It is a parable, the last of a series told to the Pharisees, who derided Jesus for his teaching on riches. It opens with the same words as the parable of the unjust steward. Taken literally it has bodies in the grave, a tongue cooled by a drop of water, and talk across a gulf between Abraham's bosom and torment. Its point is its last line: those who will not hear Moses and the prophets will not be persuaded though one rose from the dead, as the rulers were not when Lazarus and then Jesus rose.

points.claim: It is told to the Pharisees in a series of parables.
It opens as the parable of the unjust steward does, "There was a certain rich man."
Its point is unbelief despite a resurrection, fulfilled when the rulers plotted to kill Lazarus after he was raised.

objections.objection: Jesus does not call it a parable.
objections.answer: Nor does he the prodigal son or the unjust steward, told in the same discourse.

entries.subject: death
entries.title: Ecclesiastes 12:7, "the spirit shall return unto God", read as the soul going to heaven
entries.summary: The spirit (ruach) is the breath of life God gives, which man and beast have alike: "they have all one breath." At death the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the breath to God who gave it, as it was put into Adam's nostrils. The same book says the dead know not anything. The breath is God's, given and taken back, not a conscious man.

points.claim: Man and beast have one breath and go to one place.
God gives the breath and takes it back, and man returns to dust.
When the breath goes, his thoughts perish; the dead know not anything.

entries.subject: death
entries.title: Matthew 10:28, "not able to kill the soul", read as an immortal soul
entries.summary: Soul (psuchē) is life: two verses on, "he that findeth his life shall lose it" uses the same word. Men can take this life, but not the life God will give at the resurrection, which is hid with Christ. God can destroy both soul and body in the valley of Hinnom: the soul can be destroyed, so it is not immortal, and the end is destruction, not torment. Luke's account has it: fear him which after he hath killed hath power to cast into the valley of Hinnom.

points.claim: Psuchē is translated life in the same passage.
The life men cannot take is the life to come, given at the resurrection.
God can destroy the soul; Luke speaks of being killed and then cast into the valley of Hinnom.

entries.subject: death
entries.title: Matthew 25:46, "everlasting punishment", read as eternal torment
entries.summary: The punishment is everlasting, not the punishing: Paul calls it "everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord." The contrast is with life eternal, so the punishment is its loss, death that is never undone. The "everlasting fire" is the fire that burned Sodom, which is not burning now, and the wages of sin is death.

points.claim: The punishment is everlasting destruction.
The contrast is life against perishing and death.
Everlasting fire is Sodom's, which turned the cities to ashes.

objections.objection: "The smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever" (Revelation 14:11).
objections.answer: These are Isaiah's words on Edom, whose smoke "shall go up for ever," and which then lies waste with owls and ravens dwelling in it. The fire did its work and was gone; the smoke is the lasting witness of the judgment.

entries.subject: death
entries.title: 2 Corinthians 5:8, "absent from the body, present with the Lord", read as going to heaven at death
entries.summary: Paul says what he longs for: not to be unclothed, but clothed upon, "that mortality might be swallowed up of life." That is the change at the resurrection, when "death is swallowed up in victory." The chapter before says he who raised Jesus will raise us and present us with you. To be absent from this mortal body and present with the Lord is to be changed at his coming; the next verses go straight to the judgment seat of Christ.

points.claim: Paul does not want to be unclothed, but for mortality to be swallowed up of life.
Mortality is swallowed up at the resurrection.
He looked to be raised and presented with them, and to stand at the judgment seat.

entries.subject: death
entries.title: Philippians 1:23, "to depart, and to be with Christ", read as going to heaven at death
entries.summary: The dead know not anything: to the one who dies, the next moment is the resurrection, and so to depart is, to him, to be with Christ. In the same letter Paul looks to attain the resurrection of the dead, and waits for the saviour from heaven to change his body. Near his death he said his departure was at hand and his crown laid up for "that day," of Christ's appearing. "So shall we ever be with the Lord" is said of the coming, not of death.

points.claim: Paul's hope in the same letter is the resurrection, when Christ comes from heaven.
His crown is given at Christ's appearing, not at his departure.
Believers are with the Lord from his coming.
The dead know nothing, so death and resurrection are, to them, one moment.

entries.subject: death
entries.title: 1 Peter 3:18-20, "preached unto the spirits in prison", read as Christ preaching to the dead
entries.summary: Christ was quickened by the spirit, "by which also he went and preached" in the days of Noah, while the ark was preparing. The spirit of Christ spoke in the prophets, and Noah was a preacher of righteousness. Those who heard and did not obey are now in prison, in the grave. Peter says the same in the next chapter: the gospel was "preached also to them that are dead": dead now, alive when they heard it.

points.claim: The preaching was by the spirit, in the days of Noah.
The spirit of Christ spoke through the prophets; Noah preached righteousness.
The gospel was preached to those who are now dead.

entries.subject: death
entries.title: Matthew 11:14, "this is Elias, which was for to come", read as reincarnation
entries.summary: The angel said John would go before the Lord "in the spirit and power of Elias", not as Elijah born again, and when he was asked, "Art thou Elias?", John said, "I am not." Elijah was taken up in a whirlwind; he did not die to be reborn. Jesus' "if ye will receive it" marks a figure: John fulfilled Malachi's promise by doing Elijah's work, turning the hearts of the fathers to the children.

points.claim: John came in the spirit and power of Elijah.
John denied that he was Elijah.
Elijah was taken up in a whirlwind, not born again.
Jesus said it as a figure, for those who would receive it.

entries.subject: death
entries.title: Jeremiah 1:5, "before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee", read as the soul living before birth
entries.summary: God knew Jeremiah before he was formed as he knows all his purpose beforehand, "calling those things which be not as though they were": in his book all David's members were written "when as yet there was none of them." Man began when God formed him: "Yahweh God formed man of the dust of the ground, ... and man became a living soul." Jacob and Esau, "being not yet born, neither having done any good or evil," had no life before.

points.claim: God knows and calls what is not yet, as though it were.
His people are foreknown and chosen in his purpose, not alive in heaven.
Man began when he was formed, and became a living soul.
Before birth there is no deed, good or evil.

objections.objection: God "sanctified" and "ordained" him then; he must have existed to be ordained.
objections.answer: Christ himself was "foreordained before the foundation of the world, but was manifest in these last times": God appoints in his purpose what he brings about in its time.

entries.subject: death
entries.title: 1 Corinthians 3:15, "saved; yet so as by fire", read as purgatory
entries.summary: The fire tries each man's work, what he built on the foundation, not his soul, and it comes in "the day," when the Lord comes and makes manifest the counsels of the hearts. A teacher whose converts fall away loses his reward but is saved himself, as one escaping through a fire. The blood of Christ "cleanseth us from all sin": by one offering he has perfected for ever them that are sanctified, and "there is no more offering for sin." The dead know not anything, and no prayer is made for them in Scripture.

points.claim: The fire tests works built on the foundation, and the day that declares it is Christ's coming.
Christ's blood cleanses from all sin; nothing is left to be purged after death.
The dead know nothing; there is no work or device in the grave.
Prayer cannot change the state of the dead: David ceased to fast when the child died.

objections.objection: 2 Maccabees 12 commends prayer and sacrifice for the dead.
objections.answer: Maccabees is not Scripture: it was never in the Hebrew Bible Jesus called "the law, the prophets, and the psalms," and its writer asks pardon if he has written "slenderly and meanly." Even there Judas offers for the dead in hope of their resurrection, not their release from fire.

entries.subject: adversary
entries.title: The adversary is sin, not a fallen angel
entries.summary: Christ through death destroyed the false accuser, which had the power of death: he did it in his own flesh, where God condemned sin. Every man is tempted when drawn away by his own lust; evil comes from within. In the Bible "adversary" is an ordinary word: Yahweh raised up Hadad as an adversary to Solomon, his angel stood as an adversary to Balaam, and Jesus called Peter one. Judas was a false accuser, and the same word is used of slanderous women.

points.claim: Christ destroyed the false accuser by his death, condemning sin in the flesh.
Temptation and evil come from within a man.
"Adversary" is used of men and of an angel of Yahweh; "false accuser" of Judas and of slanderers.
Yahweh is the source of both good and calamity: there is no rival power.

objections.objection: Lucifer fell from heaven (Isaiah 14:12).
objections.answer: The chapter is a proverb against the king of Babylon, "the man that made the earth to tremble." Lucifer is the morning star, his boast of himself.

objections.objection: The serpent in Eden was the devil.
objections.answer: It is called a beast of the field, and cursed above all cattle.

entries.subject: adversary
entries.title: Demons are the old name for madness, illness and idols, not fallen spirits
entries.summary: The Gospels speak in the language of their day. The boy "lunatick and sore vexed" in one verse has a demon cast out of him in the next; the Jews said Jesus "hath a demon, and is mad." Healed, the man possessed sat "in his right mind." Jesus rebuked a fever and the wind as he rebuked demons. In the law and in Paul, demons are the gods of idols, which are nothing, and Zechariah foretells the unclean spirit passing out of the land with the idols and false prophets.

points.claim: Demon-possession and madness or illness are used of the same cases.
Jesus rebuked a fever and the sea as he rebuked demons.
Demons are the gods of idols, and an idol is nothing.
The unclean spirit departs with the idols and false prophets.

objections.objection: The demons spoke, and knew who Jesus was.
objections.answer: The sick spoke, in the belief they held about themselves; the man of the tombs said "my name is Legion" as a madman would. That Jesus was the Christ was known and spoken of across Galilee.

objections.objection: The demons went into the swine.
objections.answer: The madness passed to the swine as Naaman's leprosy passed to Gehazi: the disease went where God sent it, and the herd ran into the sea.

entries.subject: adversary
entries.title: Matthew 4:1-11, the temptation in the wilderness, read as a fallen angel tempting Jesus
entries.summary: The adversary in the wilderness was a delegation of the Jewish leaders. They had sent to John's baptism to ask who he was, had seen Jesus declared the Son of God, and wanted him on their side to lead a revolt against Rome. The kingdoms offered were the tetrarchies of Israel, his if he would bow to them as their puppet king. It was a crown without the cross: Jesus refused it, as he later refused the crowd that would make him king by force, and Peter, whom he called an adversary for the same counsel.

points.claim: The rulers had sent priests and Levites to John's baptism, and the declaration from heaven was public.
The land was divided into tetrarchies, the kingdoms the adversary claimed to give.
Kingship without the cross was offered again, and refused again, and Peter was called an adversary for urging it.
He was tempted as we are; God tempts no one, and Christ was not tempted by a power beyond the human.

objections.objection: He was shown all the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time.
objections.answer: No mountain shows them to the eye: they were shown in the offer. Luke's word for the world (oikoumenē) is the inhabited land, the same word used of Augustus' census that took in Judaea.

entries.subject: adversary
entries.title: Job 1:6-12, the adversary before Yahweh, read as a fallen angel with power over men
entries.summary: The adversary in Job has no power of his own: everything he does is given by Yahweh and bounded by him. Yahweh says to him, "thou movedst me against him," and at the end Job's friends comfort him over "all the evil that Yahweh had brought upon him." After the second chapter the adversary is never mentioned again; Job and his friends speak only of God. He is one who came among the worshippers to accuse Job of serving God for gain.

points.claim: Every power he has is given by Yahweh, and bounded by him.
Yahweh owns the evil: "thou movedst me against him"; "the evil that Yahweh had brought upon him."
His charge is that Job served God for gain.
Yahweh is the one source of good and evil; there is no rival.

entries.subject: adversary
entries.title: Ezekiel 28:12-19, the anointed cherub in Eden, read as the fall of an angel
entries.summary: The lament is "upon the king of Tyrus," whom Ezekiel has just told, "thou art a man, and not God." Tyre's king was set high, wise and rich, as the cherub covering the mercy seat, and walked in a garden of God's blessing. He fell "by the multitude of thy merchandise" and was brought to ashes before all that beheld him: the sins and the end of a trading king, not of an angel.

points.claim: It is spoken to the king of Tyre, a man.
He fell through his trade and the pride of his riches.
He was turned to ashes on the earth before men.

entries.subject: adversary
entries.title: Revelation 12:7-9, war in heaven, read as an angel's rebellion before creation
entries.summary: Revelation is a book of signs, and the chapter opens with "a great sign in heaven," a woman clothed with the sun. The dragon has seven heads and ten horns with crowns, which the book explains as kings and kingdoms. It is called the old serpent, the false accuser and the adversary for what it does: it deceives and accuses. It is overcome not by angels alone but by the saints, "by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony." It is a vision of things to come, not of the past: John was shown "things which must be hereafter."

points.claim: The book is signified, and the woman and the dragon are signs.
Heads, horns and crowns are kings and kingdoms.
The dragon is overcome by the blood of the Lamb and the saints' testimony.
The vision is of things to come.

entries.subject: kingdom
entries.title: The kingdom of God will be on the earth
entries.summary: God will set up a kingdom that breaks the kingdoms of men and fills the earth. Jesus will sit on David's throne and reign over Israel; the meek will inherit the earth, and the saints reign on it. The apostles asked when the kingdom would be restored to Israel, and were told the same Jesus would come again. Jesus taught us to pray that God's will be done on earth as in heaven.

points.claim: God's kingdom replaces the kingdoms of men on the earth.
Jesus will sit on David's throne.
The meek inherit the earth; the saints reign on it.
It comes at Christ's return.

objections.objection: "My kingdom is not of this world" (John 18:36).
objections.answer: Not from this world: its origin and power are not of this world's order, and "now" it was not from hence. It is not said to be elsewhere than the earth.

objections.objection: "The kingdom of God is within you" (Luke 17:21).
objections.answer: He was speaking to the Pharisees, in whom it was not. Among you: the king was standing in their midst.

entries.subject: kingdom
entries.title: The gospel was preached to Abraham: the land, for ever
entries.summary: God promised Abraham and his seed the land he walked through, for an everlasting possession. Abraham never received so much as to set his foot on, and died in faith not having received the promises. The seed is Christ, and those baptised into Christ are Abraham's seed and heirs: Paul calls the promise the gospel, and Abraham heir of the world. It is fulfilled when the faithful are raised to inherit it together.

points.claim: The land was promised to Abraham himself and his seed, for ever.
He did not receive it in his life.
The promise is the gospel; the seed is Christ, and those in him are heirs.
The faithful receive it together, at the resurrection.

objections.objection: They desired "a better country, that is, an heavenly" (Hebrews 11:16).
objections.answer: Heavenly in origin and character: the city God has prepared comes down from heaven to the earth, as the heavenly calling is a calling from heaven.

entries.subject: kingdom
entries.title: Jesus will come again, in person, to the earth
entries.summary: The angels told the apostles that "this same Jesus" would come "in like manner" as they saw him go. The heavens receive him until the times of restitution; then he comes to raise the dead, judge the living and the dead, and reign. Every eye will see him. His followers wait for him, not for death.

points.claim: The same Jesus will come in like manner as he went.
Heaven holds him until the restoration of all things.
He comes to raise the dead and judge.
Believers wait for him.

objections.objection: He returned in AD 70.
objections.answer: He came in judgment on Jerusalem then, as the prophets speak of Yahweh coming against a nation; but the dead were not raised, the saints did not reign, and the kingdom was not restored to Israel. His return in like manner as he went is still to come.

entries.subject: kingdom
entries.title: John 14:2-3, "in my Father's house are many mansions", read as rooms in heaven
entries.summary: Jesus says he will come again and receive his disciples to himself: they are with him when he returns, not when they die. The Father's house is the temple, and the house of God is the ecclesia, a building fitly framed for God's dwelling. "Mansions" (monai) are abodes, and the same chapter uses the word: the Father and the Son "will come unto him, and make our abode with him." He went to prepare the place by his death and his entry as high priest into the presence of God for us.

points.claim: He will come again to receive them.
The Father's house is the temple; God's house is the ecclesia.
The abode is God and Christ dwelling in the believer.
He prepared it by his death and by entering heaven as high priest.

entries.subject: kingdom
entries.title: 1 Thessalonians 4:16-17, "caught up ... to meet the Lord in the air", read as a secret rapture to heaven
entries.summary: Nothing is secret: the Lord descends "with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God," and the dead in Christ rise first. To "meet" him was what a city did for a coming king, going out to welcome him and returning with him, as the brethren came out to meet Paul and the virgins went out to meet the bridegroom. Jesus comes once, after the tribulation, as lightning seen by all, and his feet stand on the mount of Olives; his saints reign with him on the earth.

points.claim: His coming is open and loud, with a shout and a trumpet, and the dead rise first.
To meet him is to go out and welcome a coming king, and come back with him.
He comes once, after the tribulation, as lightning seen by all.
He comes to the earth, and his saints reign with him there.

objections.objection: "The one shall be taken, and the other left."
objections.answer: As in the days of Noah, the flood "came, and took them all away": those taken are taken in judgement. Asked "Where, Lord?", Jesus answered, "wheresoever the body is, thither will the eagles be gathered together."

objections.objection: He comes "as a thief in the night."
objections.answer: Unexpected to the world, not unseen: "sudden destruction cometh upon them," but "ye, brethren, are not in darkness, that that day should overtake you as a thief."

entries.subject: kingdom
entries.title: Revelation 7:4, "an hundred and forty and four thousand", read as a heavenly class apart from an earthly great crowd
entries.summary: The number is a sign, twelve thousand sealed from each tribe of Israel, and John turns to see "a great multitude, which no man could number," in the same vision, also before the throne and serving God in his temple. All the redeemed, of every nation, sing that they "shall reign on the earth." There is "one hope of your calling" and "one fold, and one shepherd": the faithful of old are not made perfect without the rest, but all together.

points.claim: The sealed are numbered by the tribes of Israel, a sign of the whole Israel of God.
The great multitude stands before the same throne and serves in the same temple.
All the redeemed, of every nation, will reign on the earth.
There is one hope, one flock, and the faithful are made perfect together.

objections.objection: Jesus spoke of a "little flock" to receive the kingdom.
objections.answer: The little flock is all his disciples, few beside the world, and the kingdom given them is the kingdom on the earth promised to all the saints, not a heaven for some.

entries.subject: kingdom
entries.title: No man knows the day: the dates set for his coming failed
entries.summary: "Of that day and hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels of heaven, but my Father only." William Miller set the coming for 1843 and then 1844 from Daniel 8:14; when nothing was seen, his followers said a judgement had begun in heaven instead. The Watchtower set 1874, then 1914, 1925 and 1975, and said of the first two that he had come invisibly. A word that does not come to pass is one Yahweh has not spoken. Believers are told to watch the signs and look up, not to fix the day.

points.claim: No man knows the day or hour, and it is not for us to know the times.
A prophecy that fails was not spoken by Yahweh.
His coming is seen by every eye, not invisible nor confined to a room in heaven.
Daniel 8:14 is the sanctuary trodden down by the little horn and cleansed when the desolation ends; it says nothing of a judgement begun in heaven in 1844.
Believers watch the signs and look up, ready at any hour.

objections.objection: Daniel gave numbers of days: they must be meant to be reckoned.
objections.answer: They mark the length of events once they begin, so the faithful could know where they stood; they were never given to fix the hour of his return, which Jesus said the Father kept in his own power.

entries.subject: law
entries.title: Christ fulfilled the law of Moses, and believers are not under it
entries.summary: Jesus came not to destroy the law but to fulfil it, and Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth. The law was a schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ; after faith is come, we are no longer under a schoolmaster. God promised a new covenant, written on the heart, and the first became old, ready to vanish away. Its sabbaths, feasts and foods were a shadow of things to come, but the body is of Christ; its moral teaching remains in the law of Christ, to love God and one's neighbour.

points.claim: Jesus fulfilled the law; he is its end, for righteousness.
The law was a schoolmaster until Christ; believers are not under it.
God promised a new covenant, and the first became old, ready to vanish away.
Its holy days were a shadow; Christ is the substance.
The apostles laid no burden of the law on Gentile believers, beyond a few necessary things.
Love fulfils the law; believers keep the law of Christ.

objections.objection: Not one jot or tittle shall pass from the law.
objections.answer: "Till all be fulfilled": and Jesus fulfilled it, saying on the cross, "It is finished." The law does not fail but is accomplished, as a shadow gives way to what cast it.

entries.subject: law
entries.title: Exodus 20:8-11, "remember the sabbath day", read as binding on believers now
entries.summary: The sabbath was a sign between Yahweh and the children of Israel, made known at Sinai, and Paul names it among the shadows of things to come: "Let no man therefore judge you ... in respect of ... the sabbath days." It points to the rest God has promised, which remains for his people. The disciples met on the first day of the week to break bread, and the apostles did not lay the sabbath on the Gentiles. Keeping it is no sin, but making it a test of faith adds to the gospel.

points.claim: The sabbath was a sign of the covenant with Israel.
Paul counts it a shadow, and no one is to be judged by it.
It points to God's rest, still to come.
The disciples met on the first day; the sabbath was not laid on the Gentiles.

objections.objection: The sabbath was made at creation, before Israel.
objections.answer: God rested on the seventh day, but no one is commanded to keep it until the manna in the wilderness, and Nehemiah says it was made known at Sinai.

objections.objection: It is one of the ten commandments, which stand for ever.
objections.answer: The others are taught again in the apostles' letters; the sabbath alone is not, and is called a shadow. The tables of stone are the covenant Paul says was done away, beside the ministry of the spirit.

entries.subject: salvation
entries.title: Believe the gospel and be baptised
entries.summary: The apostles preached "the things concerning the kingdom of God, and the name of Jesus Christ," and those who believed were baptised, both men and women. Baptism is a burial in water and a rising from it, sharing Christ's death and his resurrection; by it believers put on Christ, and so become Abraham's seed and heirs of the promise. Peter's first preaching ended: "Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins."

points.claim: The gospel is the things of the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ.
Those who believed were baptised.
Baptism is a burial: they went down into the water, where there was much water.
Baptised into Christ, believers are Abraham's seed and heirs.

objections.objection: We are saved by faith, not by baptism.
objections.answer: Baptism is faith's obedience: "ye are all the children of God by faith in Christ Jesus. For as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ." Peter says baptism saves, as the answer of a good conscience toward God.

objections.objection: The thief on the cross was not baptised.
objections.answer: He died before Christ, and baptism into Christ's death was commanded after it; a testament is in force only after the testator's death.

entries.subject: salvation
entries.title: All have sinned, and the wages of sin is death
entries.summary: By one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned. Sin is not illusion or ignorance but the transgression of God's law, and it springs from within, from the heart and its desires. Its end is death, not another life; the remedy is not enlightenment or detachment but forgiveness, and life from God, which he gives through the one man who overcame sin.

points.claim: Sin and death came by one man, and passed upon all.
Sin is the transgression of God's law, and all have sinned.
Sin comes from within, from the heart's desires.
Its end is death; God gives life through Christ.

objections.objection: Evil is only ignorance; we need knowledge, not forgiveness.
objections.answer: Knowledge does not cure it: Paul knew the good, and did the evil he would not. The deliverance is from God, through Jesus Christ.

objections.objection: Suffering comes from craving; end craving, and suffering ends.
objections.answer: Desire is not evil in itself: man was made to desire God and his kingdom. Lust, when it has conceived, brings forth sin, and sin, death. The cure is a new heart, and the hope is life, not extinction.

entries.subject: salvation
entries.title: Christ died for our sins, as one of us
entries.summary: God set forth Jesus to be a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness. Jesus gave his life a ransom for many; he bare our sins in his own body on the tree, and by his stripes we are healed. He died for us as one of us, sharing our nature: sin was condemned in his flesh, and he rose because death could not hold one who never yielded to it. Without shedding of blood is no remission, and the law's sacrifices pointed to his. Those baptised into his death are raised with him.

points.claim: Jesus gave his life a ransom and bore the sins of many, as the prophets foretold.
God set him forth to declare his righteousness, that he might be just and the justifier of him which believeth.
Sin was condemned in the flesh he shared; he died to it once, and lives to God.
The law's sacrifices were shadows of his; without shedding of blood is no remission.
Believers share his death in baptism, and his life.

objections.objection: No soul bears another's burden; each answers for his own sin.
objections.answer: So Ezekiel says, and it holds: Christ did not take on another's guilt as if it were his. He died as one of us, the sinless representative of a sinful race, and those who are joined to his death are forgiven for his sake. The son bearing his father's iniquity against his will is what Ezekiel denies; the Son giving his own life willingly is what Isaiah foretells.

objections.objection: God can forgive without a sacrifice.
objections.answer: He forgives freely, but in a way that declares his righteousness: sin is not overlooked but condemned, in the one man who never yielded to it.

entries.subject: salvation
entries.title: Salvation is God's gift by grace, not earned by works
entries.summary: "By grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: not of works, lest any man should boast." All have sinned, and no store of good deeds outweighs the wages of sin, which is death; eternal life is the gift of God. Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness. Faith is not idle: it obeys, is baptised and bears fruit, and faith without works is dead; but works are the fruit of being saved, not its price.

points.claim: All have sinned; none is righteous by his own deeds.
Eternal life is God's gift, by grace through faith.
Abraham's faith was counted for righteousness, before the law.
Faith obeys and works; faith without works is dead.

objections.objection: God weighs good deeds against bad on the day of judgement.
objections.answer: A judge does not acquit a thief for his kindnesses. The law curses every one that continueth not in all things written in it, and whoever offends in one point is guilty of all. Forgiveness is the only remedy, and God gives it freely in Christ.

objections.objection: Then it does not matter how we live.
objections.answer: "Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid." Those baptised into Christ's death walk in newness of life, and grace teaches them to live soberly, righteously and godly.

entries.subject: salvation
entries.title: Salvation is through Jesus alone, not by many paths
entries.summary: Jesus said, "I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me," and Peter, "there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved." The paths cannot all be true, for they contradict one another: one God or many, one life or many, a risen Christ or no cross. God winked at the times of ignorance, but now commands all men every where to repent, because he has appointed a day to judge the world by the man he raised from the dead.

points.claim: Jesus is the only way to the Father; there is no other name.
The ways men hold contradict one another, and a way that seems right can end in death.
God now commands all to repent, having raised Jesus to judge the world.
God would have all men come to the knowledge of the truth, and sends the gospel to them.

objections.objection: It is arrogant to say one way is right.
objections.answer: It would be, if the claim were ours. It is Jesus' claim, and it stands or falls with his resurrection: if he rose, he is to be heard; if not, the faith is vain, as Paul himself said.

objections.objection: What of those who never heard?
objections.answer: Knowledge brings responsibility: those who have not known God's will are not judged as those who have, and "man that is in honour, and understandeth not, is like the beasts that perish." The call is to preach to all.

entries.subject: salvation
entries.title: Acts 16:33, "he and all his, straightway", the jailer's household, read as the baptism of infants
entries.summary: Paul and Silas "spake unto him the word of the Lord, and to all that were in his house," and the jailer "rejoiced, believing in God with all his house": those baptised were those who heard and believed. Crispus "believed on the Lord with all his house," and the household of Stephanas, whom Paul baptised, "addicted themselves to the ministry of the saints." No household is said to hold an infant, and every baptism in Scripture follows belief and repentance, which an infant cannot give.

points.claim: The word was spoken to all in the house, and all the house believed and rejoiced.
The other households baptised are households of believers: Crispus's believed, and Stephanas's served the saints.
Baptism follows belief and repentance, and is asked for by the one baptised.
Baptism is a burial into Christ's death, which the one baptised chooses to share.

objections.objection: Baptism replaced circumcision, which was given to infants.
objections.answer: The circumcision Paul sets beside baptism is "made without hands," of the heart, and comes "through the faith of the operation of God": it is the believer's, not the infant's.

objections.objection: Jesus said, "Suffer little children to come unto me."
objections.answer: He laid his hands on them and blessed them; he did not baptise them. They are the pattern of the humility a believer needs: "of such is the kingdom of God."

entries.subject: salvation
entries.title: 1 Corinthians 15:29, "baptized for the dead", read as baptism on behalf of the dead
entries.summary: The verse is obscure, and Paul neither commands nor describes a rite; he argues that if the dead rise not, those who are baptised in hope of the dead's rising do so in vain, as he stood in jeopardy every hour in vain. The whole chapter answers those who said there is no resurrection. Elsewhere each one believes and is baptised for himself, and none can redeem his brother: "it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment."

points.claim: The chapter answers those who said there is no resurrection of the dead.
Baptism, like Paul's danger every hour, is pointless if the dead rise not: both are done in the hope of resurrection.
Each one must believe and be baptised for himself.
Death ends the time of choosing; judgement follows.

objections.objection: Paul mentions the practice without condemning it.
objections.answer: He names no rite and no one who did it; where Scripture speaks plainly, the righteousness of the righteous is upon him, and the soul that sins shall die. An obscure verse does not overturn the plain ones.

entries.subject: salvation
entries.title: Not all will be saved: the wicked perish, and those without knowledge remain dead
entries.summary: God gave his Son "that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life": the alternative to life is perishing, not torment, and not life for all. The way to life is narrow, "and few there be that find it." Those who know God's will are raised to judgement, some to life and some to condemnation; the wicked are punished with everlasting destruction, the second death. "Man that is in honour, and understandeth not, is like the beasts that perish": those who never knew remain in the congregation of the dead.

points.claim: The choice is life or perishing.
Not all will be saved: the way to life is narrow, and few find it.
Those who knew the will of God are raised to judgement, to life or to condemnation.
The wicked are destroyed, the second death, and burnt up root and branch.
Those without understanding remain dead, and do not rise.

objections.objection: God "will have all men to be saved": a loving God would save everyone.
objections.answer: He wills it, and calls all to repent, but men "will not come" to him for life; a love that compelled would not be love, and God does not preserve for ever those who choose death.

objections.objection: "As in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive."
objections.answer: All in Christ are made alive, "every man in his own order: ... they that are Christ's at his coming." Those in Adam die; those in Christ live.

entries.subject: salvation
entries.title: Romans 9:10-23, "Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated", read as God choosing who will be saved and who damned
entries.summary: The words were said of two nations: "Two nations are in thy womb ... the elder shall serve the younger," and Malachi said "I hated Esau" of Edom's land laid waste. Paul uses them to show God's right to choose the line of promise, and so to call the Gentiles: "Even us, whom he hath called, not of the Jews only, but also of the Gentiles." The potter remakes a vessel as a nation turns or does not, and a man may purge himself to be a vessel unto honour. God "will have all men to be saved," and "whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely."

points.claim: Jacob and Esau are two nations, and the words concern their place, not their salvation.
Paul's point is God's right to call the Gentiles, and Israel's stumbling for want of faith.
The potter shapes a vessel as it responds: a nation that turns is spared.
God wills all to repent and be saved, and the call is to whosoever will.

objections.objection: God hardened Pharaoh's heart: he chose Pharaoh for destruction.
objections.answer: Pharaoh first hardened his own heart, and God confirmed him in the way he chose; God endured him "with much longsuffering" and raised him up to show his power.

objections.objection: We were "predestinated" and chosen "before the foundation of the world."
objections.answer: God chose beforehand that there should be a people in Christ, holy and adopted, and whom he foreknew; who enters is open to all who will believe and be baptised into him.

entries.subject: salvation
entries.title: The called must hold fast to the end
entries.summary: Salvation is God's gift, and it is kept by holding fast: "we are made partakers of Christ, if we hold the beginning of our confidence stedfast unto the end." Jesus said, "he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved," and Paul kept his body under "lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway." The believer's assurance is God's faithfulness, not a past moment: he that has begun a good work will perform it, and he is able to keep us from falling.

points.claim: We are partakers of Christ if we hold fast to the end.
Those once enlightened can fall away.
Paul himself watched lest he be a castaway, and warned the standing to take heed lest they fall.
Assurance rests on God's faithfulness: he forgives the one who confesses, and keeps the one who trusts him.

objections.objection: "Neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand."
objections.answer: No one can snatch away the sheep who "hear my voice ... and they follow me"; but a sheep may stray, and the shepherd goes after it. The promise is to those who follow.

objections.objection: Then no one can be sure of salvation.
objections.answer: The believer may be sure of God, who "is faithful and just to forgive us our sins": the confidence is in his promise, held fast, not in ourselves.
